questions.question: What is the frequency counting pattern and when do you apply it?
questions.title: Frequency Counting Pattern Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: The **frequency counting pattern** uses a **hash map** (or a fixed-size array for known alphabets) to tally **how many times each element appears** in a single pass. It turns many 'count / compare / find duplicate / most common' problems from **O(n^2)** nested scanning into **O(n)** time with **O(k)** space, where k is the number of distinct elements. Reach for it whenever you need counts, duplicates, anagrams, or 'majority/top' answers.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you recognize the pattern and its O(n) time / O(k) space tradeoff over brute force
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using nested loops to count (O(n^2)) when one map pass works, or a HashMap where a 26/256 int array is faster
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention using a fixed int[26] or int[256] for known character sets instead of a HashMap

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Tally counts in **one pass** with a map or fixed array.
- Turns **O(n^2)** pair comparisons into **O(n)** time, **O(k)** space.
- Use **`int[26]`/`int[256]`** for known alphabets; HashMap otherwise.
- `merge(k, 1, Integer::sum)` is the clean increment idiom.
- Backbone of duplicates, anagrams, top-K, first-unique, palindrome-rearrange.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: The frequency counting pattern is one of the most reusable tools in interviews. The idea is simple: I make a single pass over the input and tally how many times each element appears, usually in a hash map keyed by the element with the count as the value. Once I have those counts, a whole family of questions becomes easy: detecting duplicates, checking if two strings are anagrams, finding the first non-repeating character, finding the top K most frequent elements, the majority element, or whether a string can be rearranged into a palindrome. The reason this pattern matters is complexity. A brute force approach to many of these problems compares every pair of elements, which is O of n squared. Counting frequencies first is O of n time and O of k space, where k is the number of distinct elements. So I trade a little memory for a big speedup. One refinement I'd mention: when the set of possible elements is small and known, like lowercase English letters or ASCII characters, I don't even need a hash map. I can use a fixed-size integer array, int of twenty-six for lowercase letters, and index it with the character minus the letter a. That's faster and lighter than a hash map because it avoids hashing and boxing. In Java, a clean way to increment counts in a map is the merge method, calling merge with the key, one, and Integer sum, which either inserts one or adds one to the existing count. So whenever a problem mentions counts, duplicates, most common, or anagrams, frequency counting is the first thing I reach for.

sections.title: Replace repeated scans with one count table
sections.content:
Frequency counting separates a problem into two passes: first build reliable counts, then use those counts to answer the actual question. This avoids searching the whole input again for every value.

**Example: `banana`**

Start with an empty map. Reading the characters in order produces `b=1`, `a=1`, `n=1`, then `a=2`, `n=2`, and finally `a=3`. The completed map is `{b=1, a=3, n=2}`. From the same data, code can find repeated characters, the most frequent character, or compare it with another word's counts.

Choose the storage from the key range. A `HashMap<Character, Integer>` works for an open or unknown set of characters. For guaranteed lowercase English letters, `int[26]` is simpler and avoids hashing; index `c - 'a'` stores the count. The array is not appropriate when uppercase letters, arbitrary Unicode, or general objects are allowed.

Building counts is O(n). Reading or comparing the count structure usually costs O(k), where `k` is the number of distinct keys or the fixed alphabet size. Memory is O(k). The method is useful for anagrams, duplicate detection, first unique values, majority checks, and top-frequency problems.

sections.title: Frequency Counting Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[input array/string] --> B{for each element x} B --> C[count x = count x + 1] C --> B B -- done --> D[map: element -> count] D --> E[answer the query:
duplicate? anagram?
top-K? first unique?] ```

sections.title: Counting Frequencies with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Nested loops to count**: O(n^2) when a single map pass is O(n).
- **HashMap for fixed alphabets**: an `int[26]`/`int[256]` is faster and lighter.
- **Forgetting to handle absent keys**: use `getOrDefault` or `merge`, not `get` then null-check.
- **Off-by-one with `c - 'a'`**: only valid for lowercase a-z input.

questions.question: How do you find the top K most frequent elements in an array?
questions.title: Top K Frequent Elements Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Count** frequencies in a map, then select the **top K**. Two good options: a **min-heap of size K** over (element, count) gives **O(n log K)** time; or **bucket sort** by frequency (index = count) gives **O(n)** time. Avoid sorting all counts (**O(n log n)**) when K is small. The heap keeps only the K best seen so far.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you count first, then pick top-K with a size-K min-heap (O(n log K)) or bucket sort (O(n))
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Sorting all elements by frequency (O(n log n)) when a size-K heap or bucket sort is better, or a max-heap of all n
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why a size-K MIN-heap beats a full max-heap, and offer bucket sort as the O(n) optimum

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Always **count first** into a map.
- **Size-K min-heap** -> O(n log K), the standard answer.
- **Bucket sort by frequency** -> O(n), the optimum.
- Avoid sorting all counts (**O(n log n)**) when K is small.
- A min-heap keeps the K largest by evicting the smallest.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: The first step for top K frequent elements is always frequency counting: I make one pass and build a map from each element to how many times it appears. The interesting part is how I select the top K from those counts, and there are three approaches. The simplest is to sort all the entries by frequency and take the first K, but that's O of n log n, which is wasteful when K is small. A better approach is a min-heap of size K. I push elements keyed by their count, and whenever the heap grows beyond K, I pop the smallest. The reason I use a min-heap and not a max-heap is subtle but important: with a size-K min-heap, the smallest of the current top K is always at the top, so it's cheap to evict it when a more frequent element comes along. At the end the heap holds exactly the K most frequent elements, and the total time is O of n log K, which beats full sorting when K is much smaller than n. The optimal approach is bucket sort. Since any element's frequency is between one and n, I can make an array of lists where the index is the frequency, drop each element into the bucket matching its count, and then collect elements from the highest-frequency buckets downward until I have K. That's linear, O of n time. So in an interview I'd present the size-K min-heap as my main answer and mention bucket sort as the linear-time optimization. For example, `[1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3]` gives counts `{1=3, 2=2, 3=1}`. With `k = 2`, the two highest counts belong to `1` and `2`, so the result is `[1, 2]`.

sections.title: Counts plus a size-k min-heap
sections.content:
The problem has two stages: count each value, then keep the `k` values with the largest counts. A `HashMap` handles counting, and a min-heap ordered by frequency keeps only the best `k` candidates seen so far.

**Worked example: `[1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3]`, `k = 2`**

The map is `{1=3, 2=2, 3=1}`. Add entries to the heap. Whenever its size exceeds 2, remove the smallest frequency. After all three entries, frequency 1 is removed, leaving values 1 and 2. Their output order can be arbitrary unless the problem specifies a tie or ranking rule.

The heap's root is the weakest selected candidate, so a better candidate can replace it immediately. Building the counts costs O(n). If there are `m` distinct values, heap work costs O(m log k), and storage is O(m + k).

Sorting all `m` frequency entries is simpler but costs O(m log m). Bucket sorting by frequency can reach O(n) time because no count exceeds `n`, but it uses an array of buckets. Clarify what should happen when counts tie and validate that `0 <= k <= m`; those details affect deterministic output and error handling.

sections.title: Heap-Based Top-K
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[array] --> B[count freq in map]
    B --> C{for each element, count}
    C --> D[push to min-heap by count]
    D --> E{heap size > K?}
    E -- yes --> F[pop smallest count]
    E -- no --> C
    F --> C
    C -- done --> G[heap holds K most frequent]
```

sections.title: Brute: Sort Everything - O(n log n)
Optimal: Size-K Min-Heap - O(n log K)
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Sorting everything**: O(n log n) when a size-K heap is O(n log K).
- **Max-heap of all n**: O(n + k log n); a **size-K min-heap** is better for small K.
- **Comparator direction**: for a min-heap by count use `freq.get(a) - freq.get(b)`.
- **Forgetting bucket sort**: it's the O(n) optimum since counts are bounded by n.

questions.question: How do you group strings that are anagrams together?
questions.title: Group Anagrams Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Group by a canonical key**: two words are anagrams iff they share the same key. Build the key by either **sorting each word's letters** (`O(L log L)` per word) or a **26-count signature** (`O(L)` per word), then bucket words into a `HashMap<key, List<String>>`. Total **O(n*L)** with the count-key. The map's values are the anagram groups.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you map each word to a canonical anagram key and group with a HashMap of key -> list
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Comparing every pair of words (O(n^2 * L)) instead of keying, or a count-array key without a stable string form
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Offer the O(L) count-based key (e.g. '#1#0#2...') as faster than sorting each word

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Anagrams share a **canonical key**; group via `HashMap<key, List>`.
- **Sorted key**: O(L log L)/word; **count key**: O(L)/word.
- Total **O(n*L)** with the count key.
- Convert the count array to a **String** key (arrays use identity equality).
- `computeIfAbsent` cleanly initializes each bucket.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: The core idea for grouping anagrams is to give every word a canonical key that's the same for all words that are anagrams of each other, then bucket the words by that key in a hash map from key to a list of words. Anagrams are words with the same letters in different orders, like eat, tea, and ate. There are two natural ways to build the canonical key. The first is to sort the characters of each word; eat, tea, and ate all sort to a-e-t, so that sorted string becomes the key. Sorting each word is O of L log L, where L is the word length. The second, slightly faster, way is a count-based key. I build a frequency array of the twenty-six letters for the word, then turn that array into a string, for example by joining the counts with separators. Two anagrams produce the same count array and therefore the same string key, and building it is O of L per word, avoiding the sort. With n words, the total time is O of n times L using the count key. The alternative of comparing every pair of words to see if they're anagrams would be O of n squared times L, so the keying approach is a big win. A couple of Java specifics: I can't use the int array directly as a map key because arrays compare by identity, so I convert it to a string; and I use computeIfAbsent to create each bucket's list on demand. At the end, the map's values are exactly the groups of anagrams.

sections.title: Canonical signatures turn anagrams into map keys
sections.content:
Anagrams share the same characters with the same counts. Convert every word into a canonical signature, then use that signature as a map key. Words with the same key naturally collect in the same list.

**Worked example: `[eat, tea, tan, ate, nat, bat]`**

Sorting the letters gives signature `aet` for `eat`, `tea`, and `ate`; `ant` for `tan` and `nat`; and `abt` for `bat`. The map therefore forms the groups `[eat, tea, ate]`, `[tan, nat]`, and `[bat]`.

For lowercase English letters, a 26-value frequency signature avoids sorting. It might encode `a1#e1#t1` for the first group. Separators or fixed positions are necessary so counts such as `1, 11` cannot be confused with `11, 1`. For general Unicode text, sorted code points or a map-based signature is safer.

If each word has length `L`, sorting signatures costs about O(n × L log L). Fixed-alphabet counting costs O(n × L). Both need output space plus a map of signatures.

State whether matching ignores case, spaces, or punctuation. The usual coding problem treats the strings exactly as supplied, so normalization should not be added silently.

sections.title: Canonical-Key Grouping
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[list of words] --> B{for each word} B --> C[build canonical key
sorted or 26-count] C --> D[map key -> add word to its list] D --> B B -- done --> E[map values = anagram groups] ```

sections.title: Group Anagrams with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Pairwise comparison**: O(n^2 * L) instead of O(n*L) with keys.
- **Using int[] as a map key directly**: arrays use identity equality - convert to a String.
- **Sorting when not needed**: the count key is O(L) vs O(L log L) for sorting.
- **Forgetting `computeIfAbsent`**: avoids manual null-check-then-create.

questions.question: How do you find the first non-repeating character in a string?
questions.title: First Non-Repeating Character Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Two passes**: pass one counts every character's frequency (HashMap or `int[256]`); pass two scans the string **left to right** and returns the **first character whose count is 1**. **O(n)** time, **O(k)** space. The key insight: counting must finish **before** you look for the first unique, so a single pass alone can't answer it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you use two passes (count, then scan in order) and preserve original order in the second pass
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to answer in one pass, or iterating the map (loses original order) instead of the string
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that scanning the string (not the map) in pass two preserves order; mention LinkedHashMap as an alternative

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Pass 1**: count all chars; **Pass 2**: scan string in order for count == 1.
- Must finish counting before deciding uniqueness.
- Scan the **string**, not the map, to preserve order.
- **O(n)** time, **O(k)** space.
- `LinkedHashMap` is an ordered single-structure alternative.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: To find the first non-repeating character, I use two passes over the string. In the first pass, I count how many times each character appears, using either a hash map from character to count or, since characters fit in a small range, a fixed integer array indexed by the character's code. In the second pass, I scan the string again from left to right and return the first character whose recorded count is exactly one. The most important insight here is the ordering of the work: I can't know whether a character is unique until I've seen the entire string, so a single pass that tries to decide on the fly won't work. I have to complete all the counting first, then look for the first unique. The second important detail is what I iterate in the second pass. I scan the original string, not the frequency map. A regular hash map has no defined order, so if I iterated the map looking for a count of one, I might return a unique character that isn't actually the first one in the string. Scanning the string preserves the left-to-right order the question asks for. Both passes are linear, so the time complexity is O of n, and the space is O of k for the distinct characters, which is constant if the alphabet is fixed. As an alternative, I could use a LinkedHashMap, which preserves insertion order, so I could count into it and then iterate it directly and still get the first unique correctly, all with one data structure. For example, `swiss` has counts `s=3`, `w=1`, and `i=1`. A second scan follows the original order, so `w` at index 1 is returned before `i`.

sections.title: Two passes separate counting from ordering
sections.content:
The first non-repeating character is the earliest character whose total frequency is one. One pass cannot safely return the first new character, because a later occurrence may make it repeated.

**Worked example: `swiss`**

Count all characters first: `s=3`, `w=1`, and `i=1`. Scan the original string again. `s` is rejected because its count is 3; `w` is accepted at index 1. Although `i` is also unique, it appears later.

A `HashMap<Character, Integer>` works for general character values, but its iteration order must not be used to decide “first.” The second string scan preserves the true order. For lowercase English letters, an `int[26]` is a smaller alternative. If the input may contain emoji or supplementary Unicode characters, iterate code points instead of individual UTF-16 `char` units.

Both passes together are O(n), and storage is O(k) for `k` distinct characters. Return `-1`, an empty optional, or another clearly documented value when no unique character exists. Also state whether case and spaces count; `A` and `a` are different unless normalization is explicitly required.

sections.title: Two-Pass Approach
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[string s] --> B[pass 1:
count each char] B --> C[freq map ready] C --> D{pass 2: scan s
left to right} D --> E{count of char == 1?} E -- yes --> F[return that char] E -- no --> D D -- end reached --> G[return none] ```

sections.title: First Unique Char with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **One-pass attempt**: you can't know a char is unique until all are counted.
- **Iterating the map**: a `HashMap` has no order, so it may not return the *first* unique - scan the **string**.
- **Char range assumption**: `int[256]` covers ASCII; use a HashMap for Unicode.
- **Returning index vs character**: follow the method's stated return contract.

questions.question: How do you use frequency counting to check if a string can be rearranged into a palindrome?
questions.title: Can a String Be Rearranged into a Palindrome? Frequency Counting Approach
questions.direct_answer: Count each character's frequency, then check the **parity**: a string can be rearranged into a **palindrome** if and only if **at most one character has an odd count**. Even-length strings allow **zero** odd counts; odd-length allows exactly **one** (the middle char). **O(n)** time, **O(k)** space. You never build the palindrome - just count odds.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you reduce 'can rearrange to palindrome' to the at-most-one-odd-count rule instead of generating permutations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to generate permutations (exponential), or forgetting that exactly one odd is allowed for odd-length strings
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State the rule crisply (<=1 odd count) and track odd-count parity with a toggle for an elegant O(n) check

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Palindrome-rearrangeable **iff <= 1 character has an odd count**.
- Even length -> 0 odds; odd length -> exactly 1 odd (the center).
- Count once, then count odd frequencies: **O(n)** time, **O(k)** space.
- A set **toggle** leaves only odd-count chars behind.
- Don't generate permutations - just check parity.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: The key realization is that I don't need to actually build any palindrome; I just need to check a property of the character counts. A palindrome mirrors around its center, so every character has to appear an even number of times, with one exception: if the string's length is odd, exactly one character can have an odd count and it sits in the middle. So the rule is simple: a string can be rearranged into a palindrome if and only if at most one character has an odd frequency. The brute force idea of generating all permutations and checking each one is exponential and completely unnecessary. Instead, I count the frequency of each character in a single pass, then count how many characters have an odd frequency. If that number is zero or one, the answer is yes; otherwise no. This is O of n time and O of k space. There's an elegant implementation trick: I keep a set, and as I scan each character I toggle it, adding it if it's absent and removing it if it's present. Adding then removing cancels out for even counts, so at the end the set contains exactly the characters with odd counts. Then I just check that the set's size is at most one. For example, a-a-b-b-c has c as the only odd-count character, so the set ends with just c, size one, and I can form a palindrome like a-b-c-b-a. But a-a-b-b-c-d leaves both c and d in the set, size two, so it's impossible.

sections.title: At most one character may have an odd count
sections.content:
A palindrome reads the same from both ends, so almost every character must be placed in matching pairs. An even-length palindrome requires every frequency to be even. An odd-length palindrome may have exactly one odd frequency for its center.

**Worked example: `carrace`**

The counts are `c=2`, `a=2`, `r=2`, and `e=1`. Only `e` is odd, so the letters can be rearranged as `racecar`. In contrast, `abc` has three odd counts and cannot form a palindrome.

Count characters in a map or fixed alphabet array, then count how many frequencies are odd. The answer is true when that number is at most one. It is not necessary to generate the actual permutation.

The scan is O(n), followed by O(k) work over the distinct characters, which is O(n) overall. Storage is O(k). A set can also track odd characters by adding on an odd occurrence and removing on an even occurrence; the final set size gives the same test.

Normalization belongs to the contract. A phrase such as `Tact Coa` forms `taco cat` only if spaces are removed and letters are lowercased. Do not apply those rules unless the question asks for them.

sections.title: Odd-Count Parity Check
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[string s] --> B[count each char's frequency]
    B --> C[oddCount = chars with odd frequency]
    C --> D{oddCount <= 1?}
    D -- yes --> E[can form palindrome]
    D -- no --> F[cannot form palindrome]
```

sections.title: Can Form Palindrome with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Generating permutations**: exponential and wholly unnecessary.
- **Requiring zero odds always**: odd-length strings allow exactly **one** odd char.
- **Building the palindrome**: the question only asks *if* it can be formed.
- **Case/space sensitivity**: clarify whether to normalize before counting.
